claim: Across 15 LLM judges evaluated on MTBench and DevBench (22 tasks, ~40 solution-generating models, 150,000+ evaluation instances), position bias is confirmed not to be due to random chance and varies significantly across judges and tasks.
stance_target: treating any single LLM judge's position-bias tendency as negligible or uniformly correctable across a software factory's review pipeline
scope_conditions: 15 LLM judges, MTBench + DevBench, 22 tasks, ~40 solution-generating models, IJCNLP-AACL 2025
quoted_support: Our experiments, involving 15 LLM judges across MTBench and DevBench with 22 tasks and approximately 40 solution-generating models, result in over 150,000 evaluation instances... The findings confirm that position bias is not due to random chance and varies significantly across judges and tasks.

claim: Position bias is only weakly influenced by prompt-component length but is strongly affected by the quality gap between the two compared solutions -- bias is most severe exactly when candidate solutions are close in quality.
stance_target: assuming position bias is a minor concern when evaluating close-quality code candidates in an adversarial review pipeline -- the paper shows the opposite, bias is worst in exactly that regime
scope_conditions: pairwise and list-wise LLM judge comparison settings, 2025
quoted_support: While position bias is weakly influenced by the length of prompt components, it is strongly affected by the quality gap between solutions.

claim: The study introduces three new metrics for position bias assessment -- repetition stability, position consistency, and preference fairness -- and identifies Judge-Level, Candidate-Level, and Task-Level factors contributing to the bias.
stance_target: providing concrete, reusable metrics the software factory could adopt to quantify and monitor position bias in its own adversarial review/judge infrastructure
quoted_support: This exploratory study evaluates position bias in LLM judges across pairwise and list-wise comparison settings, introducing three metrics: repetition stability, position consistency, and preference fairness... We identify Judge-Level, Candidate-Level, and Task-Level factors contributing to bias.
